content: The situational assessment provides detailed guidance on various factors to consider when establishing safe rescue and resuscitation training. This includes determining the minimum age at which children can begin learning these skills. Data from Bangladesh indicates that the average age of a person discovering a drowning victim is typically double the age of the victim. When designing training programs, it is essential to consider environmental factors such as the type of water body (e.g., rivers, lakes, oceans, wells, ponds), wave patterns, water depth, currents, and temperature. Understanding the importance of traditional rescue and resuscitation techniques, even those known to be ineffective or dangerous, is critical for community education. Target groups for training include school children (as young as 12 years or younger, depending on circumstances), swimming class participants, and individuals who frequent water leisure locations. High-risk groups include children who travel to school by boat or cross dangerous waters, passengers on unsafe ferry boats, fishermen, cliff and lobster divers, populations in detention or refugee centers, and service personnel such as police and army members. High-impact groups include parents, teachers, community leaders, health professionals, and vessel operators. Students’ knowledge levels should encompass aquatics, human physiology, first aid, language skills, swimming, self-rescue, and awareness of medical conditions. Teachers should adopt a train-the-trainer model while being mindful of potential challenges when using trainers from other countries. Training should be tailored to the resources and equipment available in the local health system. Local trainers should be selected based on factors such as gender, ethnicity, social background, availability, and the empowerment of disadvantaged groups. Once recruited and trained, trainers should undergo periodic recertification and participate in community-building events to ensure program sustainability. Measures such as sustainable funding programs and the involvement of a local course director can help retain trainers and prevent them from leaving programs to start independent teaching ventures. If necessary, train-the-trainer approaches can rapidly increase the number of trainers. Visiting trainers should adapt their teaching to local languages and needs, using interpreters to avoid translation errors and gradually transferring responsibilities to local counterparts. Interactive learning methods, such as songs, role-plays, quizzes, and self-learning, are more effective than passive class attendance. Visual information, especially when referencing recognizable local settings, is often more impactful than written materials. Training settings should be realistic and use locally sourced materials. Rotational training stations, where trainers teach small groups a single skill over a set period, can improve skill performance, which is further enhanced during scenario-based simulation training. Courses should prioritize practical content over theoretical material, with evidence-based and regularly updated content adapted to local conditions. Rescue training should emphasize the safety of rescuers and the proper use of rescue equipment. Training should begin with simple, locally sourced equipment (e.g., plastic containers) and progress to more specialized tools. Resuscitation training should focus on basic technical skills, such as ventilation (rate, time, volume) and chest compressions (rate, depth, hands-off time). Immediate mouth-to-mouth ventilation is critical in drowning cases. Guidelines from the European Resuscitation Council (ERC) provide a comprehensive basis for creating locally adapted resuscitation content. Non-technical skills, such as communication, leadership, situational awareness, feedback, and the use of communication technology, are essential components of training. Cultural and socio-economic factors, such as gender norms and social or ethnic group dynamics, should also be addressed. For example, men may not be allowed to touch women in certain cultures, and some groups may avoid physical contact altogether. Ethical dilemmas, such as teaching cardiac resuscitation in areas without ambulance systems or local healthcare providers, should be considered. Survivors of successful mouth-to-mouth ventilation generally do not require further treatment, although eight hours of clinical observation is recommended. In settings where no further care is available, teaching only mouth-to-mouth ventilation may be appropriate. Training materials should reflect the local context and be developed early in the preparation phase. Blended learning, which combines diverse methods and materials, is often the most practical solution. Sophisticated training equipment, such as mannequins or projectors, can be expensive and may not function well in hot, humid, or bright environments. Low-tech mannequins and low-cost equipment are excellent alternatives, especially for training focused on mouth-to-mouth ventilation. Smartphones, increasingly available even in remote locations, can be used for video feedback. Refresher training is necessary, as resuscitation skills retention typically lasts 3–12 months in learners who have not used the skills in real situations. Refresher courses should include hands-on cognitive and practical skills training. Posters, short videos, and interactive lectures can enhance retention. Instructors are encouraged to maintain logs of all rescues or resuscitations performed by their students and provide feedback on their performance. In Lesotho, where there is no tradition of swimming due to the lack of natural lakes and large rivers, the Royal Lesotho Lifesaving Association has implemented a training program. Students must demonstrate swimming ability before receiving training in rescue and resuscitation skills. The program includes basic, intermediate, and advanced certifications, with the final stage being the bronze medallion, which qualifies individuals to become instructors. Since 2011, approximately 480 certificates have been issued, mostly at the basic level. For water transport safety, regulatory and educational interventions are necessary. These include training crews, fostering a safety culture, and raising public awareness. Compulsory lifejacket-wearing regulations for small boats have been shown to reduce drowning deaths. However, the lack of rigorous studies highlights the need for evaluation to build an evidence base for new safety measures. Large vessel safety requires robust regulations and enforcement, as well as a commitment to safety culture. Training on safety management systems helps crews manage risks, including human and mechanical factors, tides, currents, and weather conditions. E-learning, supplemented by on-board training, is a cost-effective way to enhance proficiency. Weather detection and dissemination techniques, such as SMS-based alert systems, can reduce fatalities associated with bad weather.
